text: Jupiter's mass is about 318 times Earth's
as_written: about three hundred and eighteen times the mass of Earth
source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, Jupiter

text: Converting Jupiter's mass to energy via E=mc^2 gives roughly 1.7e44 joules, about 14 billion years of the Sun's luminosity
as_written: you would release about as much energy as the Sun puts out in fourteen billion years
source: Derived from Jupiter mass 1.898e27 kg (NASA Planetary Fact Sheet) and nominal solar luminosity 3.828e26 W (IAU 2015 Resolution B3)

text: Jupiter is about 11 times wider than Earth
as_written: Jupiter is about eleven times wider than Earth
source: NASA Jupiter facts and Planetary Fact Sheet (equatorial diameter about 142,984 km vs 12,756 km)

text: Jupiter has more than 2.5 times the mass of all other planets combined
as_written: It has more than two and a half times the mass of all the other planets put together
source: NASA Solar System Exploration, Jupiter overview

text: The Great Red Spot is wider than Earth
as_written: is wider than our entire planet
source: NASA Juno and Hubble observations of the Great Red Spot

text: Jupiter has about one thousandth of the Sun's mass
as_written: about one thousandth of the Sun's mass
source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet; IAU nominal GM values (Jupiter/Sun mass ratio about 1/1047)

text: Jupiter orbits about 778 million km from the Sun, 5.2 AU
as_written: about seven hundred and seventy eight million kilometres from the Sun, which is five point two times farther out than Earth
source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, Jupiter

text: Changes in gravity propagate at light speed; GW170817 gravitational waves and gamma rays arrived about 1.7 s apart after about 130 million light years
as_written: about a hundred and thirty million light years away
source: Abbott et al. 2017, Gravitational Waves and Gamma-rays from a Binary Neutron Star Merger, Astrophysical Journal Letters 848, L13 (LIGO, Virgo, Fermi GBM, INTEGRAL)

text: Gamma rays arrived about 1.7 seconds after the gravitational wave signal
as_written: about one point seven seconds later
source: Abbott et al. 2017, ApJL 848, L13

text: Gravity changes travel at the speed of light
as_written: Changes in gravity travel at the speed of light
source: Abbott et al. 2017, ApJL 848, L13 (speed of gravity equals c within a few parts in 10^15)

text: Closest Earth-Jupiter distance is about 588 million km
as_written: about five hundred and eighty eight million kilometres away
source: NASA Solar System Exploration, Jupiter facts

text: Farthest Earth-Jupiter distance is about 968 million km
as_written: about nine hundred and sixty eight million
source: NASA Solar System Exploration, Jupiter facts

text: Light takes about 33 to 54 minutes to cross the Earth-Jupiter distance
as_written: between roughly thirty three and fifty four minutes
source: Derived: NASA distances of 588 and 968 million km divided by c = 299,792 km/s

text: Earth orbits at about 30 km/s
as_written: Earth keeps moving at about thirty kilometres per second
source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, Earth (mean orbital velocity 29.78 km/s)

text: At closest approach Jupiter's pull on Earth is about 16,000 times weaker than the Sun's
as_written: roughly sixteen thousand times more weakly than the Sun does
source: Derived from Newtonian gravity with NASA/IAU GM values and the 588 million km closest distance

text: Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system and bigger than Mercury
as_written: it is bigger than the planet Mercury
source: NASA Solar System Exploration, Ganymede (diameter about 5,268 km vs Mercury 4,879 km)

text: Io's orbital speed is about 17 km/s
as_written: Io was moving at about seventeen kilometres per second
source: NASA JPL Planetary Satellite Physical Parameters (about 17.3 km/s)

text: At 17 km/s an object covers about 1.5 million km per day
as_written: it covers about one and a half million kilometres
source: Derived: 17.3 km/s times 86,400 s

text: Jupiter's orbital speed is about 13 km/s
as_written: at about thirteen kilometres per second
source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, Jupiter (about 13.06 km/s)

text: Solar escape speed at Jupiter's distance is about 18.5 km/s
as_written: about eighteen and a half kilometres per second
source: Derived: square root of 2 times Jupiter's circular speed of about 13.07 km/s

text: Best-case heliocentric speed of Io after vanishing is about 30 km/s (13.07 + 17.3)
as_written: Io, in the best case, would be moving at around thirty kilometres per second
source: Derived from NASA/JPL orbital speeds

text: Ganymede's orbital speed is about 10.9 km/s and in the worst case would leave about 2 km/s heliocentric speed (13.07 minus 10.88)
as_written: Ganymede, at about ten point nine kilometres per second
source: NASA JPL Planetary Satellite Physical Parameters; derived subtraction

text: Leftover heliocentric speed of a backward-moving Ganymede is just over 2 km/s
as_written: just over two kilometres per second around the Sun
source: Derived: 13.07 km/s minus 10.88 km/s

text: Jupiter Trojans lie 60 degrees ahead of and behind Jupiter at the L4 and L5 points
as_written: Sixty degrees ahead of it in its orbit, and sixty degrees behind
source: NASA Lucy mission; Lagrange point theory

text: More than 10,000 Jupiter Trojans are known
as_written: More than ten thousand are known
source: IAU Minor Planet Center Trojan asteroid listings

text: Lucy launched in 2021 to study Trojan asteroids as remnants of planet formation
as_written: NASA's Lucy spacecraft, launched in 2021
source: NASA Lucy mission

text: Europa Clipper launched October 2024 and arrives at Jupiter in 2030
as_written: Europa Clipper launched in October 2024 and is due at Jupiter in 2030
source: NASA Europa Clipper mission

text: ESA's Juice launched April 2023 and arrives at Jupiter in 2031
as_written: Europe's Juice mission launched in April 2023 and is due in 2031
source: European Space Agency, Juice mission

text: New Horizons' 2007 Jupiter flyby shortened the trip to Pluto by about three years
as_written: shaved about three years off its trip to Pluto
source: NASA New Horizons mission

text: The Sun-Jupiter barycentre is about 1.07 solar radii from the Sun's centre
as_written: about one point oh seven solar radii from its centre
source: Derived from NASA mass ratio and semimajor axis; consistent with JPL Horizons barycentre data

text: Jupiter's orbital period is about 11.86 years
as_written: every twelve years or so
source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, Jupiter

text: Sun-Saturn barycentre lies about 0.6 solar radii from the Sun's centre
as_written: only about sixty percent of the way from the Sun's centre to its surface
source: Derived: Saturn at 9.58 AU, Sun/Saturn mass ratio about 3498, solar radius 695,700 km (NASA Planetary Fact Sheet; IAU)

text: Jupiter is usually outshone only by the Sun, Moon and Venus
as_written: Jupiter is usually outshone only by the Sun, the Moon and Venus
source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet apparent magnitudes; Astronomical Almanac

text: Babylonian astronomers tracked Jupiter's motion more than 2,000 years ago
as_written: more than two thousand years ago
source: Ossendrijver 2016, Science 351, 482 (Babylonian tablets dated 350 to 50 BCE)

text: Jovian electrons reach Earth's vicinity with a modulation of about 13 months, the Earth-Jupiter synodic period of about 399 days
as_written: roughly every thirteen months
source: Teegarden et al. 1974, Journal of Geophysical Research 79, 3615; Ulysses and SOHO electron observations; NASA synodic period data

text: Jupiter contributes about 154 arcseconds per century to Mercury's perihelion precession, second only to Venus
as_written: about one hundred and fifty arcseconds per century, second only to Venus
source: Clemence 1947, Reviews of Modern Physics 19, 361

text: Relativistic precession of Mercury is about 43 arcseconds per century
as_written: about forty three arcseconds per century
source: Einstein 1915; Clemence 1947, Reviews of Modern Physics 19, 361

text: Jupiter's contribution (about 154) is more than three times the relativistic part (about 43)
as_written: more than three times bigger
source: Derived from Clemence 1947

text: The total mass of the asteroid belt is less than Earth's Moon
as_written: All of it together weighs less than our Moon
source: NASA Solar System Exploration, Asteroids

text: Daniel Kirkwood identified gaps in the asteroid belt in 1866
as_written: In 1866, an astronomer named Daniel Kirkwood noticed
source: Kirkwood 1866 (announced) and 1867, Meteoric Astronomy

text: The 3:1 Kirkwood gap lies at about 2.5 AU
as_written: about two and a half times Earth's distance from the Sun
source: Bottke et al. 2002, Icarus 156, 399

text: The 3:1 resonance with Jupiter is a major source of near-Earth asteroids
as_written: A study led by William Bottke found that the three to one gap is one of the main routes into the inner solar system
source: Bottke et al. 2002, Debiased Orbital and Absolute Magnitude Distribution of the Near-Earth Objects, Icarus 156, 399

text: Near-Earth asteroids survive a few million years before impact, solar plunge or ejection
as_written: lasts only a few million years
source: Gladman et al. 1997, Science 277, 197

text: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 impacted Jupiter in July 1994 as more than 20 fragments over six days
as_written: In July 1994, a comet called Shoemaker Levy 9, which Jupiter had torn into more than twenty pieces, slammed into the planet over six days
source: NASA/JPL Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 impact records

text: Amateur astronomers have recorded multiple impact flashes on Jupiter since 2010
as_written: Since 2010, amateur astronomers have caught several more flashes from smaller impacts
source: Hueso et al. 2010, Astrophysical Journal Letters 721, L129 and later reports

text: Jupiter and Saturn are near a 5:2 resonance (five Jupiter orbits roughly equal two Saturn orbits)
as_written: Five Jupiter orbits take almost exactly as long as two Saturn orbits
source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet orbital periods (11.86 and 29.46 years); Murray and Dermott, Solar System Dynamics

text: The Great Inequality has a period of roughly 900 years
as_written: The beat repeats about every nine hundred years
source: Laplace, Mecanique Celeste; Murray and Dermott, Solar System Dynamics

text: Earth's present orbital eccentricity is about 0.017 and varies from near 0 to about 0.06
as_written: off circular by about one point seven percent
source: Berger and Loutre 1991, Quaternary Science Reviews; Laskar et al. 2004, A&A 428, 261

text: Earth's eccentricity ranges from almost zero to about six percent
as_written: from almost zero to about six percent
source: Berger and Loutre 1991; Laskar et al. 2004, A&A 428, 261

text: A roughly 405,000-year eccentricity cycle arises from Venus-Jupiter interaction
as_written: about every four hundred and five thousand years
source: Laskar et al. 2004, A Long-term Numerical Solution for the Insolation Quantities of the Earth, Astronomy and Astrophysics 428, 261

text: Earth's axial tilt is stabilised mainly by the Moon
as_written: steadied mainly by the Moon
source: Laskar, Joutel and Robutel 1993, Nature 361, 615

text: Laskar 1989 showed chaos in the inner solar system with errors growing about tenfold every ten million years
as_written: multiply by about ten every ten million years
source: Laskar 1989, Nature 338, 237

text: Laskar published the inner solar system chaos result in 1989
as_written: In 1989, the French astronomer Jacques Laskar
source: Laskar 1989, Nature 338, 237

text: Wetherill suggested in 1994 that a Jupiter-less system would suffer more comet impacts on Earth
as_written: In 1994, the planetary scientist George Wetherill published calculations
source: Wetherill 1994, Astrophysics and Space Science 212, 23

text: Simulations show Jupiter helps against long-period comets but may increase asteroid impacts; effect on in-between bodies is mixed
as_written: For long period comets, Jupiter does help.
source: Horner and Jones 2008, 2009 and Horner, Jones and Chambers 2010, Jupiter - friend or foe? series I to III, International Journal of Astrobiology

text: Some simulations suggest Earth would be hit less often by asteroids without Jupiter
as_written: some of their simulations suggest Earth would be hit less often without Jupiter
source: Horner and Jones 2008, Jupiter - friend or foe? I: the asteroids, International Journal of Astrobiology 7, 251

text: 51 Pegasi b was the first planet found around a Sun-like star, in 1995, by Mayor and Queloz
as_written: in 1995, by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz
source: Mayor and Queloz 1995, Nature 378, 355

text: 51 Pegasi b orbits in about 4.2 days
as_written: orbits its star every four days or so
source: Mayor and Queloz 1995, Nature 378, 355

text: Exoplanet searches have been running about three decades since 1995
as_written: Astronomers have spent three decades counting
source: Derived from Mayor and Queloz 1995

text: Jupiter analogues occur around roughly 6 to 14 percent of Sun-like stars
as_written: roughly six to fourteen percent of Sun-like stars
source: Wittenmyer et al. 2016, ApJ 819, 28 (about 6 percent); Fernandes et al. 2019, ApJ 874, 81 (about 14 percent)

text: About 26 percent of Sun-like stars host a 1 to 2 Earth-radius planet on a 5 to 100 day orbit
as_written: about one in four Sun-like stars hosts a planet one to two times Earth's width on a close orbit
source: Petigura, Howard and Marcy 2013, PNAS 110, 19273 (Kepler)

text: Jupiter induces a Sun velocity wobble of about 12.5 m/s
as_written: about twelve and a half metres per second
source: Fischer et al. 2016, State of the Field: Extreme Precision Radial Velocities, PASP 128, 066001

text: Saturn induces a Sun velocity wobble of about 2.8 m/s
as_written: about two point eight
source: Fischer et al. 2016, PASP 128, 066001

text: Earth induces a Sun velocity wobble of about 9 cm/s
as_written: about nine centimetres per second
source: Fischer et al. 2016, PASP 128, 066001
